claims.claim: Le Guin reports that The Song of Roland has four thousand lines containing one simile and no metaphors.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: The Song of Roland has four thousand lines, containing one simile and no metaphors.

claims.claim: Le Guin says Homer's metaphors may be extended but are neither static nor ornate.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: they are neither static nor ornate

claims.claim: Le Guin says the style, of course, is the book, and that this is absolutely true of fantasy.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: The style, of course, is the book.

claims.claim: Le Guin says that if you remove the style all you have left is a synopsis of the plot.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: all you have left is a synopsis of the plot

claims.claim: Le Guin says that from the writer's point of view the style is the writer.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)

claims.claim: Le Guin observes that give-and-take conversations in Dunsany tend to be very brief, as they do in the Bible.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: tend to be very brief, as they do in the Bible

claims.claim: Le Guin says the touchstone of plausibility in imaginative fiction is probably coherence.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Plausibility in Fantasy: an open letter to Alexei Mutovkin" (2005)
claims.quote: The touchstone to plausibility in imaginative fiction is probably coherence.

claims.claim: Le Guin says the rules governing how things work in an imagined world cannot be changed during the story.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Plausibility in Fantasy: an open letter to Alexei Mutovkin" (2005)
claims.quote: cannot be changed during the story

claims.claim: Le Guin says fiction validates itself through accurate, honest observation of the world it creates.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Plausibility Revisited: Wha Hoppen and What Didn't" (2005), ursulakleguin.com
claims.quote: accurate, honest observation of the world it creates

claims.claim: Le Guin says what constitutes plausibility in fantasy is the coherence of the story and its consistent self-reference.
claims.quote: the coherence of the story, its consistent self-reference

claims.claim: Le Guin names the unfed, unwatered horses of lazy fantasy as a symptom of a world that has not been imagined.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Some Assumptions about Fantasy" (BookExpo America, 4 June 2004)
claims.quote: nobody there ever feeds or waters their horses

claims.claim: Le Guin asks whether reviewers ever consider that the meaning of a story might lie in the language itself rather than in a tidy bit of advice.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "A Message About Messages", CBC Magazine, 2005 (text at ursulakleguin.com)
claims.quote: the meaning of the story might lie in the language itself

claims.claim: Le Guin says most rules of what is currently trendy or supposedly salable are hogwash.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigation Q1: How do you make something good?", Book View Cafe, 27 July 2015
claims.page: paragraph on the pressure of opinion

claims.claim: Le Guin says magnitude dilutes the emotional effect of a literary massacre, a mutilated corpse or two making us flinch where a thousand orcs in agony leave us unmoved.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2, Round 1", Book View Cafe, 2016
claims.quote: a thousand orcs in agony leave us unmoved

claims.claim: Le Guin recommends thinking of a story as an organic whole in which the beginning will imply the end and the end will fulfill the beginning.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2, Round 1", Book View Cafe, 2016
claims.quote: the beginning will imply the end

verdicts.trueWording: The Song of Roland has four thousand lines, containing one simile
verdicts.note: Raw PDF p.8 (epic-language paragraph): sentence ends '...and no metaphors.' Quote word for word; both limbs (four thousand lines; one simile, no metaphors) on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Homer's metaphors may be extended, but they are neither static nor ornate
verdicts.note: Raw PDF p.8, same paragraph, sentence immediately before the Roland sentence. Quote 'they are neither static nor ornate' verbatim; 'may be extended' limb also present.

verdicts.trueWording: The style, of course, is the book ... absolutely true of fantasy
verdicts.note: Raw PDF p.9 (cake/frosting paragraph). Quote verbatim; the second limb is carried by the following paragraph, 'This is partly true of history; largely true of fiction; and absolutely true of fantasy.'

verdicts.trueWording: If you remove the style, all you have left is a synopsis
verdicts.note: Raw PDF p.9, same paragraph as 810; sentence ends 'of the plot.' Quote verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: From the writer's point of view, the style is the writer
verdicts.note: Raw PDF p.9, paragraph beginning 'In saying that the style is the book.' Quote verbatim; reader/writer contrast intact.

verdicts.trueWording: they tend to be very brief, as they do in the Bible
verdicts.note: Raw PDF p.5, Dunsany paragraph: 'Genuine give-and-take conversations are quite rare ... and when they occur they tend to be very brief, as they do in the Bible.' Quote verbatim; the Dunsany attribution limb is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: The touchstone to plausibility in imaginative fiction is probably coherence
verdicts.note: Raw page, paragraph beginning 'The touchstone to plausibility'. Quote verbatim. Minor: the claim paraphrase says 'touchstone OF plausibility' where the page reads 'touchstone TO plausibility' - the quoted string itself matches.

verdicts.trueWording: in the imagined world cannot be changed during the story
verdicts.note: Raw page, last sentence of the coherence paragraph: 'The rules that govern how things work in the imagined world cannot be changed during the story.' Quote verbatim; all limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: most notably through accurate, honest observation of the world it creates
verdicts.note: Raw page, second body paragraph: 'What validates fiction is plausibility, which it creates for itself, most notably through...'. Quote verbatim. The claim compresses two steps (plausibility validates; fiction creates that plausibility itself) into 'fiction validates itself' - supported, not overstated.

verdicts.trueWording: plausibility in fantasy is the coherence of the story, its consistent self-reference
verdicts.note: Raw page, fantasy paragraph, final sentence beginning 'What constitutes...'. Quote verbatim; both limbs (coherence; consistent self-reference) present.

verdicts.trueWording: why nobody there ever feeds or waters their horses
verdicts.note: Raw page, Assumption 2 ('Fantasy Land is the Middle Ages'), sentence ends '...which run all day and night just like a Prius.' Quote verbatim; the 'world not imagined' limb is carried by the same paragraph's contrast between 'a genuinely imagined society and culture' and 'this lazy-minded, recycled hokum'.

verdicts.trueWording: the meaning of the story might lie in the language itself
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'Does it ever occur to such reviewers that ... rather than a tidy bit of advice?' Quote verbatim; interrogative form and the 'tidy bit of advice' limb both present. Locator drift only: it is the SECOND body paragraph, not the third.

Raw page, paragraph beginning 'On the other hand, the pressure of opinion'. Quote verbatim; 'such rules' refers back in the same paragraph to 'the rules of what's currently trendy, the rules of what's supposed to be salable', so both limbs hold.

verdicts.trueWording: a thousand orcs in agony leave us unmoved
verdicts.note: Raw page, answer to Lauren (question 5). Quote verbatim, preceded by 'a mutilated corpse or two may make us flinch'. One modality gap worth flagging: Le Guin hedges - 'There seems to be a relationship' and 'if the magnitude ... dilutes its emotional effect' - where the claim asserts the dilution flatly.

verdicts.trueWording: the beginning will imply the end
verdicts.note: Raw page, answer to Isaac (question 2): 'I recommend thinking of a story as an organic whole, in which the beginning will imply the end and the end will fulfill the beginning.' Quote verbatim; recommendation, organic-whole and both directional limbs all present.
